weather.name: NOAA hourly weather
weather.method: measured hourly dry-bulb; years beyond 2024 replay the 2015-2024 cycle

demand.name: Team demand model (heat_models.py)
demand.method: gradient-boosted quantile regression on NREL ComStock/ResStock hourly heat (held-out hourly R2 0.94); per-type shapes for each real weather year x each building's annual heat
datasets: NREL ComStock AMY2018 r3 (NY County, Tompkins)
assumptions: use type -> NREL building type mapping in ml/team_ml.py
greenhouse / aquaculture keep the degree-day physics profile (no NREL type)
stress scenarios shift space heat by the shape's own degree-hour slope
p05/p95 = model's hourly P10/P90 spread for the whole service area

supply.name: Team supply model (heat_models.py)
supply.method: site 1: LL84 monthly electricity regression (IT vs cooling) + Google-trace compute profile; site 2: proposed phase 1 AI-inference simulation
assumptions: scale = config: team shape scaled to the site config capacity
p05/p95 = team P10/P90 across simulated runs

assumptions: electricity and fuel price x U(0.8, 1.2)

site.name: Lansing, New York
site.subtitle: Heat from the proposed Lake Hawkeye data center for Lansing
site.network_owner: a Town of Lansing / TeraWulf joint venture
site.estimated_note: no benchmarking data, so its heat use is modeled from county property records (floor area, age, heating fuel)

parties.risk: Carries only the cost of its own connection. Its cooling is protected by the bypass and its own plant, so it takes none of the customers' risk.
parties.responsibility: Builds and maintains the export heat exchanger, pumps and bypass valve; keeps its own cooling plant independent and at 100% size.

parties.party: Town of Lansing + TeraWulf heat venture
parties.role: Owns heat pumps and tie-ins, runs the network, sells the heat
parties.risk: Carries demand risk (a big customer leaves), fuel-price risk (customers' alternatives get cheaper) and electricity-price risk for the heat pumps.
parties.responsibility: Owns and runs the heat pumps, heat exchangers and meters; keeps the tier promises; refunds customers for missed guaranteed hours.

parties.role: Pays for the shared street pipes
parties.risk: Capital at risk if few customers join. The benefit is public (carbon), not a cash return.
parties.responsibility: Pays its share of the street pipes as a grant.

parties.party: Greenhouse, fish farm and households: base
parties.role: Pays for heat only, keeps its boiler as backup
parties.risk: Lock-in to one heat supplier; protected by price below today's cost, backup boiler, and refunds for missed hours (firm and protected tiers).
parties.responsibility: Allows the connection, pays the heat bill, keeps its boiler serviced.

parties.role: Sets the rules, receives the public benefit
parties.risk: Carbon and air benefits only appear if customers actually connect.
parties.responsibility: Permits the pipes, sets the tier rules and the affordability guarantee.

match_scorecard.headline: All of the heat is used directly: no heat pump needed
match_scorecard.how: The data center's water is at about 50 C. Low-temperature users (greenhouses, radiant floors, new buildings, mild-weather radiators) take it directly. Hot water (60 C) and cold-weather radiators get a heat pump that lifts only the difference, so the less lift, the less electricity.

match_scorecard.headline: Peak export 2.3 MW against 72.0 MW available (3.2%)
match_scorecard.how: Checked for every hour of 12 typical days: the heat customers can draw never exceeds what the data center can give. Each heat pump covers only part of its building's coldest hour; the boiler covers the rest.

match_scorecard.headline: Winter export is 92% flat across the day (average / peak)
match_scorecard.how: Computers make heat all day. Homes peak morning and evening, offices by day, hotels and hot-water users run through the night. Mixing them flattens the draw so it matches a flat supply; the tiers decide who goes first if it ever does not.

match_scorecard.headline: 3% of the data center's heat is used in winter, 1% in summer; 55% of delivered heat is year-round load
match_scorecard.how: Heating demand follows the weather; hot water and process heat (such as a greenhouse) do not. Customers are chosen with their summer baseload in mind, so the summer heat is used rather than wasted.

match_scorecard.headline: 99.91% expected network availability; every customer keeps its boiler
match_scorecard.how: Expected time off the network comes from failure rates (data center trip, a break on the customer's own pipe path, building equipment). Storage rides through short trips, valves isolate a broken branch, and the customer's boiler starts by itself within about 10 minutes. Protected and firm customers are the last to be cut when supply is short.

rules.rule: Export is a second sink, never the only one
rules.how: The data center keeps its own heat-rejection plant (air-cooled dry coolers, as designed) sized for 100% of its heat, with its own redundancy. HeatOS adds a free extra place for the heat to go. Nothing about its cooling design depends on us.

A fail-open valve sits between the data center's loop and the network. If the network trips, loses flow or runs hot, the valve sends all the water back through the data center's own coolers within about 30 seconds. The data center's temperature setpoint is never changed by us.

rules.rule: Never export more than 80% of the heat
rules.how: Its own coolers always carry a base load and stay warm and tested. In this plan the peak hour exports 2.6% of the heat, so the rule is met.
A plate heat exchanger keeps the data center's coolant apart from the network water, so a pipe leak outside cannot reach the computers.

Customers take heat out, so the water that comes back is cooler than what went out. That is free pre-cooling for the data center and the reason the plan frees cooling electricity (see the data-center benefits).

# HeatOS: Lansing data center heat reuse

*Generated 2026-10-03 23:40 from the live HeatOS model.*
*Pitch: Data center heat that neighbors can count on, with a price for that certainty.*

> **Data status.** Data providers: buildings: Team building inventory, weather: NOAA hourly weather, demand: Team demand model (heat_models.py), supply: Team supply model (heat_models.py), confidence: mock, jev: OpenJev (openjev-latest)
> Every number below is computed by the model; the source of each input is listed in Appendix A. Inputs marked "assumption - verify" are placeholders to be confirmed.

---

## 1. Decision framework: where heat reuse should go first

HeatOS scores both candidate sites on nine weighted criteria (1-5 scale).

| Criterion | Weight | Chelsea | Lansing | Why |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Demand density | 10% | 5 | 2 | dense multi-family and commercial blocks vs dispersed rural users |
| Source temperature | 10% | 3 | 5 | air-cooled 27-32 C vs liquid-cooled 45-65 C |
| Supply continuity | 10% | 3 | 3 | colocation tenants vs crypto-exposed flexible load |
| Cost of heat displaced | 10% | 5 | 4 | Con Ed steam and oil vs propane and oil |
| Infrastructure cost per MWh | 15% | 3 | 3 | street works in Manhattan vs long rural runs |
| Carbon displaced | 10% | 4 | 4 | steam/gas on a 0.25-0.44 t/MWh grid vs propane/oil on a cleaner grid |
| Local air / water / noise | 10% | 5 | 3 | PM2.5 92nd percentile block vs clean rural air |
| Vulnerable people served | 15% | 5 | 2 | public housing towers next door vs no disadvantaged communities |
| Community acceptance leverage | 10% | 3 | 5 | heat as a host-community benefit for a contested data center |
| **Weighted total** | 100% | **4.00** | **3.35** | |

**Robustness.** Across 100,000 random re-weightings (Dirichlet, alpha = weight x 40) with +/-0.75 noise on every score, **Chelsea ranks first in 96.6% of draws**. Recommendation: **Chelsea**.

Within the chosen site, a building connects only if its best option has a positive 20-year value (financial NPV at 6% plus avoided CO2 at $190/t), and only while the data center has firm capacity left. Buildings are added in priority order: NPV x (1 + equity score) x boiler urgency.

## 2. Data analysis

### Datasets and models
| Component | Method | Datasets | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Team building inventory | LL84 benchmarking + PLUTO (Chelsea), parcels + OpenStreetMap (Lansing), via the team's optimize.py | NYC LL84 annual benchmarking, NYC PLUTO, Tompkins County parcels, OpenStreetMap | v0.1 |
| NOAA hourly weather | measured hourly dry-bulb; years beyond 2024 replay the 2015-2024 cycle | NOAA ISD global-hourly 72505394728 (Central Park), NOAA ISD 72515594761 (Ithaca Tompkins Regional) | vISD 2015-2024 |
| Team demand model (heat_models.py) | gradient-boosted quantile regression on NREL ComStock/ResStock hourly heat (held-out hourly R2 0.94); per-type shapes for each real weather year x each building's annual heat | NREL ComStock AMY2018 r3 (NY County, Tompkins), NREL ResStock AMY2018 r1 (NY), NOAA ISD 2015-2024, NYC LL84 (annual heat, site 1), Tompkins parcels (site 2) | vHistGBR quantile |
| Team supply model (heat_models.py) | site 1: LL84 monthly electricity regression (IT vs cooling) + Google-trace compute profile; site 2: proposed phase 1 AI-inference simulation | NYC LL84 monthly (111 8th Ave), Google powerdata_2019 traces, NOAA ISD 2015-2024 | vcalibrated sim + Monte Carlo |
| Mock confidence engine | 100 futures, uniform jitter, engine simulator | engine simulator outputs | MOCK (teammate model pending) |
| OpenJev (openjev-latest) | typed System One decisions read from model probabilities | live network state rendered as text | v0.5 |


### Building inventory (88 candidates)
| Heating system | Buildings | Annual heat (MWh) |
|---|---:|---:|
| propane | 88 | 25,085 |


### Recommendation (2 buildings connected)

Not connected: 86 buildings with no option of positive value; 0 worthwhile buildings waiting on capacity. Firm capacity used: 3,373 of 12,282 kW.

### Key modelling assumptions
- Heat pump COP = eta x T_hot / (T_hot - T_cold), eta 0.6 (range 0.5-0.8).
- Energy balance closes every simulated hour within 0.1%; a full year simulates in under a second.
- Autopilot: rules (data center heat, then storage, then existing boilers) or MPC (48 h linear program minimizing electricity + fuel + carbon).
- Full parameter list with sources: Appendix A.

## 4. Risk assessment

| Risk | Type | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation | Owner | Linked stress test | Modelled result |

| Lake-effect cold snap | Climate / technical | Medium | Medium | Pit storage sized for seasonal shifting; boilers kept at each user | Joint venture | lake effect cold snap | backup +0 MWh/week vs normal; storage used 0 MWh; guaranteed missed hours 0 |
| Crypto price crash switches off flexible load | Market | High | Medium | Heat contracts on the firm (non-flexible) share; pit storage bridges | TeraWulf | bitcoin price crash | backup +0 MWh/week vs normal; storage used 0 MWh; guaranteed missed hours 0 |
| Greenhouse operator off-season or exit | Commercial | Medium | Medium | Pit absorbs surplus; schools and homes phase in | Joint venture | greenhouse off season | backup -0 MWh/week vs normal; storage used 0 MWh; guaranteed missed hours 0 |
| Data center outage | Technical | Low | Low | Pit storage ride-through | TeraWulf | server outage | backup +0 MWh/week vs normal; storage used 22 MWh; guaranteed missed hours 0 |
| Electricity price spike | Market | Medium | Low | Mostly direct use; only boosters use power | Homes co-op | price spike | backup +0 MWh/week vs normal; storage used 0 MWh; guaranteed missed hours 0 |

| Cayuga Lake nutrient / thermal impacts | Environmental | Low | High | Closed loops; aquaculture effluent treated; monitoring (verify) | Joint venture | - | - |


**Confidence.** Over the next 48 h, P(all connected buildings fully served by the network) = 100%; expected hours on backup 0.0; top uncertainty drivers: Building heat demand 97%, Electricity price 3%, Heat pump efficiency 0% (40 futures, mock_uniform_jitter).

## 5. Implementation vision

### Phase 1: Built-in from day one
TeraWulf's liquid cooling exports 45-65 C water through a heat export station.
Buildings: Greenhouse (Proposed, 5 Acres).

### Phase 2: Greenhouse park and pit storage
Greenhouses, aquaculture and schools take warm water directly; the pit on the remediated coal yard shifts summer surplus to winter.
Buildings: Indoor Fish Farm (Proposed).

### Phase 3: Homes co-op
Home clusters along the loop join a co-op; small booster heat pumps make hot tap water, financed on the bill.


### Who pays, and does everyone come out ahead?
| Party | Upfront | Financed | Annual operating | 20-yr NPV | Payback | P(ahead) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| TeraWulf (data center) | $3,121,631 | $0 | $2,081,021 | $20,747,519 | 2 | 100% |
| Joint venture (TeraWulf + Town of Lansing / Tompkins County) | $5,417,139 | $0 | $577,418 | $1,205,797 | 10 | 81% |
| Greenhouses, aquaculture and schools | $0 | $0 | $275,082 | $3,155,168 | 0 | 100% |
| Homes co-op | $0 | $0 | $0 | $0 | 0 | 100% |


**Everyone wins?** Yes: every party is ahead in at least 80% of 16 sampled futures with the configured terms.

## Appendix B: how each headline number is computed
- **Site scores**: engine/site_scoring.py: weights and scores in CRITERIA; robustness = 100,000 Dirichlet draws
- **Recommendation**: engine/recommend.py: per-option 20-yr NPV at the site discount rate + avoided CO2 x carbon price
- **Heat, backup, electricity**: engine/physics.py + engine/sim.py: hourly simulation with energy balance checked every hour
- **Net CO2**: engine/impact.py: fuel displaced x fuel factor - (heat pump + pump electricity) x grid + chiller electricity avoided x grid
- **Water**: engine/impact.py: evaporation = heat (MJ) / 2.26; tower water = evaporation / 0.67; minus 2 gal per kWh of added electricity
- **Party economics**: engine/ledger.py: hourly money flows, capex by party (pipe = minimum spanning tree), NPV at each party's rate
- **Everyone wins / guarantee premiums**: engine/guarantees.py: sampled futures through the simulator; premium = E[refunds] + CVaR95 margin
- **Stress-test results**: engine/scenarios.py: 7-day runs from 12 Jan (heat wave: 10 Jul), stress fired at hour 24, rules autopilot
